subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION

speechtext: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 98, respecting the north Pacific pelagic sealing convention.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1911 a convention was entered into between Great Britain, the United States of America, Japan and Russia in regard to pelagic sealing in the north Pacific ocean. The convention was ratified by the British parliament of the time, and later, in 1912, enabling legislation was passed by this parliament. But the enabling legislation did not provide for any sanctions for violations of the provisions of the act, and so from 1912 to the present day the sanctions provided by the Fisheries Act were applied. It has been found that this was leading to [DOT] misunderstanding by the natives of the Pacific coast, and accordingly it has been thought advisable to recast the legislation relating to pelagic sealing in the north Pacific ocean to provide sanctions for violations of the act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT POINT RESPECTING STATEMENT ON APRIL 6 OF MR. LACROIX (BEAUCE) ON QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to mention a matter of privilege affecting this house. Yesterday I endeavoured to follow the observations which were made by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix), and while I realized that he was speaking about a question of timber limits and timber dues in the province of Quebec, not until I saw this morning the translation of his observations was I able fully to grasp their meaning. It will be observed from a reading of them that they had to do with matters entirely within the province of Quebec; but that is not the point which I desire to mention. We all have an interest in the maintenance of our institutions, and I do not claim to have any greater concern in that regard than any other member of this chamber. But I invite the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to look at that translation and ascertain whether he does not think that, after a conference with the hon. member for Beauce, certain observations should be expunged from the record. I will not even mention what they are, but they are of such a character as, translated, must convince any of us that had the Speaker been able to hear what was being said he would have indicated that those observations should not have been made in this chamber, because they cannot but have, I believe, a very serious effect upon the position of the House of Commons itself. I refrain deliberately at this time from making any reference to the language employed and the charges that have been made against those who are not in this place, about matters that have nothing to do, under our federal constitution, with this house. I think that when the hon. member for Beauce has perused them, as translated in the official record, and the Prime Minister has done the same, they will regard my observations as temperate and moderate and made for one purpose only, namely to do at least what we can to maintain in this generation respect for our institutions, which I think is a very heavy obligation that rests upon each and all of us at this time

subtopic: POLLING OF VOTE OF GERMAN NATIONALS IN CANADA WITH RESPECT TO AUSTRIA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: POLLING OF VOTE OF GERMAN NATIONALS IN CANADA WITH RESPECT TO AUSTRIA
speechtext: I noticed in the press this morning a short item dealing with the question of an endeavour being made to poll the vote of German nationals in Canada with respect to the annexation of Austria. Possibly it may be of value, as some conclusions have been arrived at, if the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) would indicate whether or not (1) any effort has been made on the part of the German government to have us provide facilities for a poll being taken; (2) what reply the administration made to such request, and (3) whether any steps have or can be taken to ascertain whether or not those who claim the right to vote have been naturalized in some instances as British subjects. The latter question is perhaps of the most pressing importance from the standpoint of the country as a whole. I did not get an opportunity to indicate to the Prime Minister that I intended to ask this question on the orders of the day, and if he thinks that it is inadvisable to make an answer without further consideration he can treat it as notice; but inasmuch as the press report indicated that some conclusions had been arrived at, I assumed that possibly the question of notice was unimportant.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, April 6, consideration in committee of the following proposed resolution-Mr. Rogers-Mr. Sanderson in the chair:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide assistance towards the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress, and for such payments out of moneys appropriated by parliament as may be necessary for all or any of the purposes of the proposed legislation.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Before the committee rose yesterday afternoon the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) was engaging in a speech of rhetorical excellence, an excellence which I could not hope to approach, let alone equal; however, I might endeavour to emulate him. At that time he was engaging in a criticism as spirited in manner as it was broad in scope, of the work and contribution of the Department of Labour in reference to this problem of unemployment. According to him, it would seem that the Department of Labour is very much like Nazareth of old, out of which apparently no good could come. It seems to me pertinent to remark that just as those who condemned that village were in egregious error, so too the hon. member may very well be in error no less egregious in seeking to belittle the work and the contribution of the minister of that very difficult department.

Relief and Agricultural Distress

I do not intend to attempt anything in the way of an oratorical performance to be placed in juxtaposition in the journals of this house with the hon. gentleman's speech of yesterday, but I do think it is desirable that some facts should be dispassionately stated which perhaps might invite renewed reflection upon this problem so that possibly the result may hereafter be less emotion and a little more reason in forming and passing judgment.
I think it perhaps unnecessary for me to remark that I am by no means a complacent person. Whenever I have remarks to make they will not be solely of approbation of tilings done and of things as they are. I regard smug complacency as of greater danger in the national life than an absolute vice.
It seems to me that extensive criticism with regard to the lack of concrete proposals in the speech of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) is at the moment ill-timed. It ill becomes me to be dogmatic or didactic about such a matter, but merely from a reading of the resolution and from some slight knowledge of the place which a resolution of this sort occupies in the proceedings of parliament, I take it that we are discussing a resolution only intended to indicate the need for something being done, namely the spending of money; a resolution which under our parliamentary system is necessary in view of the fact that money is to be spent; a resolution which merely directs attention to a condition and to certain circumstances. All that is necessary, therefore, for the mover of such a resolution to do, is to speak in such a way as to give a general review of the situation. It is only necessary that the scope of the problem should be indicated rather than that details of remedies should be given; and perhaps in view of the broad scope of this problem it is not even desirable that an attempt to give full details should be made. If I might borrow a medical term, the remarks of the mover of a resolution of this sort should be diagnostic; no criticism lies because of the lack of complete disclosure of the various remedial plans. And full disclosure will come shortly when the bill is before us.
But while the minister may not have indicated exactly the measures to be taken, I apprehend that no one else is precluded from pointing out the steps that should be taken; and this is exactly what the hon. member for Greenwood did not do. As a matter of fact it is what I propose to do in presenting to the committee the ideas that occur to me-and I am going to present those ideas in complete and untrammelled freedom.
I have read with interest and profit both the interim report and the other publications of
[Mr. Maybank.l
the so-called Purvis commission, and I have also read the final report. I must say I cannot see the force of the criticism offered by the hon. member for Greenwood when he satirically utters with tragic intonation the word "final"-"final, final"-with reference to this report. It seems to me this report shows a highly creditable discharge of an onerous and important duty. The job being done, what would the members do but write finis to their work Any person who completes a job. investigative, consultative and advisory in its nature, makes a report. The fact that it is a final report is surely nothing sinister; there is nothing sinister in the dissolution of the commission. If the government should do nothing about the report and nothing about the problem, that would be a different matter.
For my part I should like to see every proposal of the so-called Purvis commission put into effect. I think the housing plans advocated by the commission in its interim report should have been put into effect. I note that the report has certain negative proposals and certain positive ones. As an illustration of a negative proposal I might mention the remarks regarding the unwisdom of certain types of public works. But we should take the report as a whole and look upon its recommendations as complementary one to the other. We ought not to fall into the error of accepting the negative recommendations and failing to accept the positive. For instance, I endorse every word that has been written or spoken in respect to the desirability of a national housing and slum clearance scheme. If that proceeds I care not at all about the other public works which the commission does not favour.
In reference to unemployment I am a strong believer in a works policy so far as possible. I hold it to be true that the curse put upon Adam has since become the most cherished privilege of the human race. That man must earn his bread in the sweat of his brow is to-day a privilege. We are accustomed to speak of unemployment as the greatest national problem; and sometimes to repeat this seems almost trite. Yet that enforced idleness is the most serious national problem not only of this country but of almost all countries cannot be gainsaid. Long idleness undoubtedly makes clods out of sentient men and women.
Ill fares the land, to hastening ills a prey,
Where wealth accumulates, and men decay-
-said Goldsmith. We have not so much evidence of wealth accumulating, but we have had for a number of years a great deal of evidence that men decay as a result of idleness. Like many other hon. members I

Relief and Agricultural Distress
have kept a scrapbook, and a short time ago I clipped a little piece from the Atlantic Monthly, which I quote:
The thing that numbs the heart is this:
That men cannot devise
Some scheme of life to banish fear
That lurks in most men's eyes.
People with numbed hearts, with a fear of unemployment so great that it lurks in their eyes, cannot develop themselves fully and cannot make the contribution which they would and shouid make to the development of the human race. In the light of all this it can never be trite to observe once more that unemployment is our greatest national problem.
So far our critics and ourselves are in agreement. But one might infer, in listening to the hon. member to whom I have referred, with his spirit of criticism, that we, in this corner and on the other side of the house, are not sensible of the transcendent nature of this problem. It is worth while to recall again that since this government took hold there has been, chiefly as a result of the scientific manner in which the problem has been handled, a steady improvement. And, per contra, when the government of the chief of the hon. member to whom I have referred were in office, in consequence of having promised to cure unemployment absolutely and forever so that it would be completely forgotten, by reason of the hit and miss manner in which the problem was then handled it grew steadily worse.
The hon. member mentioned the farm placement scheme. The minister had said that as a result of the operation of that scheme large numbers had been taken off relief; I have not the figures before me. but the hon. member for Greenwood himself mentioned the figure of 50,000. He then sought to detract from the work and the contribution of this government by saying that this was not a scheme of the present government at all, that in fact his own party was the progenitor of the scheme. It will not be amiss to remind the hon. member that it is not enough to have a plan; what is really important is the manner in which the plan is executed. It is not enough to be a progenitor. Most people I think will agree that Doctor Dafoe has been of more value in the development of the healthy lives of the Dionne quintuplets than the progenitor. Dionne may not say so, an hon. member on my left remarks, but looking at it impartially I think we give more credit to Doctor Dafoe than to Mr. Dionne. The fact is that the plan I refer to is not really the plan of the former government either. That plan emanated from Manitoba and a great deal of
51952-133i
pressure had to be put on the then government before they could be got to adopt it. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader), who sits in this house probably more than any other single person, is responsible for the adoption of that plan. He popularized the idea and " sold " it to a large extent to the Manitoba government; the Manitoba government in turn brought pressure to bear on the then federal government, and that is how that plan came to be instituted.
Great emphasis is placed upon this problem in its relation to youth. It is said that unemployment among youth is perhaps the most serious aspect of this problem. With that I am in entire agreement. Undoubtedly there are thousands of young men rapidly reaching man's estate who have never experienced the blessing and discipline of labour. Every person needs the discipline of work, and he who has not been trained under that discipline, and the thinking which practically always in some degree accompanies useful toil is handicapped in meeting the emergencies of life. It is worth while to remind ourselves that a very great and important part of the problem of unemployment among returned men is due to a youth-period engaged otherwise than in preparation for useful toil. Idleness is even worse in this respect than the war. The soldier did have some discipline, although perhaps not the best kind to fit him for commercial and industrial life. But idleness is a negation of all discipline. It encourages attack upon every idea which is a bulwark of civilization.
It may be worth while to remind the committee at this time of the blessing Canada enjoys in the character of her youth, and the difference between them and the youth of many other countries. In many countries youth is practically delivered over to designing people who have made of them in some cases tools of oppression, and also directed them into mass action of one kind and another provocative of strife. They have been Hitler-ized here, nazified there; in another place made fascist; and in one country they have been made the spearhead of an anti-God ideology. Contrast that with our own youth in this country. Everywhere we have our young people banded together in councils and societies, spending their time and boundless energy, turning their fresh minds and buoyant spirits not towards the mere accomplishment of any selfish aims but in an endeavour to make contributions to the national life of this country, to do something of lasting benefit to all. The contrast between Canadian youth and the youth of some of the other countries to which I have referred is very
210S

Relief and Agricultural Distress
great indeed. For instance, our youth are appearing at almost every sitting of the Rowell commission, in each case presenting to that commission some contribution that is worth while and beneficial to Canada as a whole. Likewise they are appearing before other public bodies presenting their views and in general influencing public opinion all over this country towards an appreciation of those things which in this nation are for the general good of all. In no case have we any such youth associations in this country engaged in the furtherance of anything that is harmful to the national life.
Personally I rejoice that the government which I support has seen the need of doing something towards the training and reclamation of youth, and I rejoice that now much more is to be done. It does not matter how much the government spends-

speechtext:
I am sorry to interrupt
some of the conversations that are going on. To continue, it does not make any difference how much money the government may spend on youth training and reclamation schemes; it is quite probable that I will not be satisfied, that I will think more should be spent. Frankly I know that I am greedy in respect to this matter; that my wants are insatiable.
But while we are considering this problem, thinking what ought to be done and endeavouring in this way to indicate what I think should be done, I am bound to contrast my ideas with those expressed in the speech of the hon. member for Greenwood yesterday, and to recall the high point of imagination set by the party which he now supports in their handling of the youth problem at that time. Then the high-water mark of imagination in dealing with this problem was to herd youth of all kinds, all types, all trainings and all ages into camps. Work? No; they did not even put them to work. They went into camps, miscalled labour camps, and they were completely without the beneficial discipline of labour. Had that system persisted it would have been the greatest crime ever perpetrated against youth in this country and the greatest crime that could have been perpetrated against the youth of any country, the most reprehensible policy any government ever put in force. The efficiency of those camps has been stated at times 
to have been in the neighbourhood of twenty-five to thirty per cent, but I visited many of those camps and I can say that it was much less than that. The youth of that day, under the aegis of the governmental scheme, neither played nor worked. There was a premium on idleness and sloth and all the rest of the things that result from that sort of treatment. Yet to hear the hon. member yesterday one would think he wanted us to go back to what according to him were the halcyon days of 1932, 1933 and 1934, when the unemployed youth prepared to march on Ottawa; when lives were lost in riots, and when something like $53,000 was spent in a commission of investigation, after it was all over. Sometimes there is criticism of the appointment of commissions. Well, I can say this, sir. It is a great deal better to appoint a commission to investigate a problem in advance, with a view to endeavouring to treat a problem in a scientific manner, than it is to wait until some harm results and then appoint a commission to investigate the difficulty that has arisen through your own acts.
In conclusion I should like to stress once more certain statements I have already made in this house. In my opinion the government should take over the unemployment problem in the main as its own burden, and relieve the cities and municipalities. The condition of my own city, and many more, indeed constitutes a national emergency. If a government contributes at all to the cost of unemployment relief it is because the matter is viewed as a national emergency. Now we have always admitted that unemployment is a national emergency, yet handling the problem in such a way that a municipality which gets its money only by direct taxation, and chiefly by direct taxation upon homes, must pay as high as fifty per cent of the total cost, is not a handling of the problem in a way that can be called national. I would say, take over the unemployment problem at any rate as far as the employables are concerned, leaving the unemployables if you will. The load in respect to them will be heavy enough, because it has increased greatly in these last few years. Thousands have been rendered unemployable by reason of the very long unemployment period they have gone through. The present condition is chilling to all enterprise. The brink of insolvency for the municipality is so close; the tax load, and the threat of an additional load, is so great that as a matter of fact people are beginning to fear the ownership of property. Hence

Relief and Agricultural Distress
there cannot be the building and improvements in the cities which otherwise probably would be the case.
This prompts me to say that in my opinion it would be highly desirable to spend money on all feasible schemes of rehabilitation in order to restore people to the work rolls. Aside from the purely human aspect of that matter it would be good business financially. A person who is allowed to slip from the class of employables into the class of unemployables becomes for many years, perhaps for the rest of his life, a threat to balanced budgets, to the extent of $500 or $1,000 per year. He may not be a threat to the balancing of the budget of the dominion government, but he is bound to be a threat to the balancing of budgets somewhere. After all, the problem is that of the people of Canada as a whole, not merely a problem of the people in relation to the jurisdiction of this dominion government.
I welcome everything that can be done with reference to the development of the trans-Canada route and the aids to the tourist business. I believe a very great deal of employment can be created by such plans. I also think it would be good business to deal with the railway question with a view to endeavouring to prevent unemployment there, and preventing further threats of lay-offs. If the general recommendations of the report are implemented I believe we may look forward hopefully, possibly not to a cure, but to a very considerable alleviation of the problem. We can then depend upon a longterm policy, the success of which, of course, would to some extent depend upon crops, of which we are always living in hope. Indeed it would seem as if the Lord has decided not to look sideways any longer upon that part of the country from which I come, and that the people west of Winnipeg, out in the great wheat empire of Saskatchewan, may probably next year be making their usual immense contribution to the economy of the country.

Mr. Chairman, I feel very sympathetic indeed towards the people in the areas of the west where great drought has been experienced. I realize, too, that we in the east may not fully appreciate the hardships which they have had to face and which they are experiencing possibly to a greater degree to-day. But I must add that I also appreciate the deplorable conditions existing in some parts of eastern Canada, especially in Ontario.
The minister stated that great numbers of people in the stricken areas had been moved to other parts of the country. Where did they go? I can tell you where some of them are;
they are in Ontario. I know of some such families who have had to be cared for by the people of Hamilton within the past few months. One case in particular comes to my mind. A man and his family, with farm stock, were moved to Wentworth county. He did not like the property on which he was placed, and as a result was moved to another. After being on the second farm only a short time he sold the stock and used the money from the sale as the first payment on a house and property in the city of Hamilton. He has had to be kept by the city ever since; and Hamilton can get no relief from Saskatchewan for these people. Many similar cases are being dealt with in Hamilton.
I have before me a file containing information with respect to several unfortunate cases, but upon this occasion I do not propose to put the details on record. But the problem is a serious one so far as Hamilton is concerned; and the same condition exists in other cities of Ontario. Yet when eastern cities apply to the federal authorities for consideration in connection with increased relief costs, they are turned down flat.
In 1935 we were told to vote for King and get action. As other hon. members have1 indicated, we have had nothing but most decided inaction. All the government has done has been to tear down and destroy the social reforms of the last administration.
What did the Liberal campaigners tell us in 1935? They said that with all provincial governments except one being Liberal, the return of a Liberal government to Ottawa would bring about a condition of unity and cooperation and make of Canada a veritable political paradise. What has been the result? There is more disunity and interprovincial ill-feeling in Canada to-day than there has been at any other time since confederation.
Unemployment insurance should have been adopted immediately, because the sooner it becomes effective and the sooner we pass through the initial stages of operation, the better. Great Britain adopted a scheme several years ago; where is she to-day? There could not be a major depression in Great Britain, because with her reserves of unemployment insurance the working man is assured of being able to meet his necessary obligations, and the internal trade of the country must at all times remain fully active.
Grants in aid are indeed necessary in some parts of the west, because we know that the people out there do need relief. But the working man in industrial centres finds himself in the position of losing his home, through lack of work, and is not receiving any grant

Relief and Agricultural Distress
in aid. Nor does he receive any assistance through home owners' creditor arrangements, to help him reclaim his home. If he finds himself out of work he must go on relief and accept the bare necessities of life. He may lose his home and be thrown out on the street.
During the course of his speech the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) stated that there was not enough of a falling off in employment to justify a change of policy; then at a later point he urged that we avoid excessive pessimism. How can one help being pessimistic when he realizes that in the city of Hamilton alone there are 600 more heads of families on relief now than there were two months ago? The minister stated he had made a thorough study of conditions. What has this government done in addition to making studies? We have had commissions, commissions, commissions-and now we are waiting for the report of another commission, which we may receive late in the year.
The minister said that the tourist trade might afford a way out of unemployment. With all the resources of a country of 11,000,000 people, is it possible that we must turn parasitic in order to exist as a nation? Are we to be another Bermuda, offering lilies, onions and trinkets? He stated further that the provinces seemed reluctant to cooperate. I would say that the reverse is the truth, and that the federal government has been the [DOT]reluctant body. In a speech last fall in support of a candidate in the vicinity of Kingston the minister said, in effect, that while Mr. Hepburn disagreed with him on some matters, he hoped Mr. Hepburn would be returned to power so that there would be that unity between Ottawa and Toronto which was so essential. I believe the minister is not in a proper state of mind to cooperate with Ontario in relief problems. He may be at variance with the premier of that province, but that should not prevent him from cooperating to the fullest extent. When the mayors met in Ottawa some three weeks ago and endeavoured to place the facts before the minister, apparently they obtained no results. Mr. Hepburn is reported to have said that the relief problem as put forward by the Minister of Labour some few days ago was to him "a headline and a headache," and he is also reported to have used these words: "I must confess I am not in the confidence of the government at Ottawa."
That is a condition which should not exist. Men in public office, in the more important departments of government, should not permit such a condition to exist. They should get down to business and make an effort to co-

operate, because the poor people throughout the country are suffering while they quibble.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I would urge that the Minister of Labour turn his attention more to the urgent needs of the great cities and towns of Ontario and the east generally; and finally I would remind him that Nero fiddled while Rome burned.

Mr. Chairman, the resolution before the committee finds its origin in action taken in this parliament two years ago in the passing of an act intituled "An act respecting the establishment of a national employment commission." It will be recalled that on that occasion there was a definite discussion of the unemployment and distress problems of Canada, and many definite expressions of opinion were given. I recall very well, and perhaps the committee will do me the honour of recalling it also, that on that occasion I warned the government that the appointment of a commission as proposed in the then bill was not a solution of the problem of unemployment or of the problems of economic distress peculiar to the country at that time. I further stated that the employment commission could not possibly report within less than eighteen months. I was too optimistic, Mr. Chairman, because it has taken two years for the commission to make its final report.
I also warned the government at that time that in all probability, when the report was made, it would not show much progress towards a practical solution of the problems with which we were confronted. I do not wish to detract in any way from the splendid public service that has been given by those who constituted the commission, from its chairman down, but I must say, after reading the report very carefully over the week-end, that it appeals to me in this way, that the commission actually should have commenced where they ended. That is, the report really shows that we have spent two years educating this commission to an understanding of the problem. I will not deny that there are e idenees in this report that the members of the commission now understand the problem of unemployment in Canada-that is, understand the extent of it, its nature and the way it works. But I can find nothing in the report, nothing of any importance, that discloses an understanding of the causes of unemployment.
But unemployment, as we have it, is an effect, and not a cause. It is the result of certain forces operating in our economic structure. The duty of the commission was to

Relief and Agricultural Distress
take the facts, which we knew then quite as well as we know them to-day; to study with the assistance of their experts the causes that lay behind, and then come to the government with their conclusions so that the government could present to parliament some definite proposals for remedying these problems.
I am not in the confidence of the government and I do not know what it is intended to bring before parliament as a result of this resolution. But I have some experience in parliamentary procedure and I draw from the resolution certain inferences which I imagine are fairly accurate. For instance, the resolution has one word in it which discloses completely the comprehension of the government of this problem, and that word is "alleviation." In other words, Mr. Chairman, the whole policy of the government as disclosed in this resolution is to be for the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress. From a humane point of view that is highly commendable, but from the standpoint of a two years' effort to understand the problem, and with tens of thousands of dollars spent upon the commission, it is not very encouraging to those who are the victims of these undisclosed causes. Surely after two years-after nearly ten years, as a matter of fact; for the unemployment problem started in 1928-surely after eight or ten years we do not need ti be told by the commission in a report of some scores of pages a number of things such as it sets out-that registration was desirable, for instance. Of course it was, and we all knew that when they started. We all appreciated that registration and the classification of the unemployed into employables and unemployables, and so forth, was desirable. Every member knew it, and it is more or less an insult to every member of this house to suggest, after two years, that we need to be told that you must divide the unemployed into different classes. We knew it then- all of us knew it.

promoters was in relation to the commission. The preamble is a guide to the interpretation of the clauses of the act. My hon. friend from Essex East (Mr. Martin) shakes his head, but I am bound to say the preamble is an indication and a guide to the interpretation of the clauses of the act. The preamble reads:
Whereas unemployment has been for several years Canada's most urgent national problem-
Then it goes on to say that something shall be done:
-to find ways and means of providing remunerative employment, thus reducing the numbers at present on relief .	.	. and whereas, to
achieve a nationwide cooperative effort in reducing the numbers on relief and in providing employment-
Not to discover that it is advisable to have cooperation, but to achieve a nation-wide cooperative effort, and:
-such nation-wide cooperative effort can best be effected through the appointment of a representative national commission, with power to cooperate with the provinces, municipalities and other agencies in respect of unemployment relief, and in an endeavour to provide work for the unemployed.
In an endeavour to provide work for the unemployed-that is in the preamble.
Now I turn to the powers of the commission. I shall not read the sections because the minister read them himself and others have referred to them. A number of powers are outlined, and then in section 7 we have this additional power which the minister said the other day the commission did not have.
Section 7 reads:

of the people that by the appointment of this commission two years ago we were to have an administrative effort by the government and the commission, working with the provinces and the municipalities, to solve these problems, and to deal with the causes of unemployment as well as the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress. It is not good enough to come to this chamber after two years have gone by and say, "Well, we have had some expansion of external trade". I will give the minister credit for consistency at least in this respect, that two years ago, and again to-day, he tied himself to external trade as the solution of our internal economic problems. What I tried to point out two years ago, and what I wish to emphasize now, is that while external trade is highly desirable, it is not a solution of the internal economic problems of this or any other democratic country. What good is it to say to the more than fifty thousand railway workers who have been thrown out of their occupations in the last few years, "Well, with external trade growing there is some hope of your being reemployed." In only partial degree is their unemployment due to the falling off of trade; because during the years that have just passed, and accelerated no doubt by the orders for larger units of motive power in the shops of the locomotive construction companies, the unemployment of these men has been largely due to changes in methods of transportation, and an increase in the number of automobiles. But let us see what it really amounts to. It shall not be said through any oversight on my part that I am belittling assistance to youth. let us examine the figures a little more closely. The employment of those youths in forestry was the result of one of the most disgraceful things that have happened in this country, hundreds, thousands of young men crowded into the city of Vancouver, penniless and destitute, without food or shelter. They stood on the street comers

with tin cans, trying to collect money; they were arrested by the hundreds and sent to gaol for thirty, sixty, ninety days. There was such an outcry in the province by public-spirited people, by the churches, boards of trade and other institutions, that these camps, about which we hear so much, to the closing of which hon. members referred a little while ago, were-some of them-reopened.	Day
after day, as I sat in my office in Vancouver during the cold, rainy days of late October, November and December, I saw hundreds of men standing around the street from eight o'clock in the morning until four o'clock in the afternoon; half and even two-thirds of them could not get to the registry gates and had to come back the next day and stand around for hours again.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Where are they now?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Some of them went to
the camps. Those camps were reopened not because of the foresight and goodwill of the government or the commission, but under duress, because of the indignation of public-spirited citizens of Vancouver who felt that these young men were entitled at least to some chance of earning their own living. I walked among these men and questioned them. Possibly a few of them were reckless characters, but I know this, after questioning dozens of them, that I found but one desire, the desire for a job. The first thing I did was to shake hands with them and feel their hands to see whether they were chaps who were willing to work; for you can tell when you shake hands with a man whether he is one who will work or will not work. I would say that ninety per cent of them ask for no more than an opportunity to work. Hon. members may smile, but I say to the minister that he cannot take credit for having opened forestry camps. The province of British Columbia opened the camps; they were supported with assistance from the minister only after public opinion was so much aroused and expressed with so much indignation that something had to be done.

I am speaking from

Relief and Agricultural Distress

I am telling him of the agitation that occurred before these young men were sent to the camps.
The minister laid great emphasis on unity, and I notice that the extent of the unity which had been achieved was apparently this. He spoke with great feeling of the difficulties of getting the dominion and the provinces together, and he emphasized the point that it was necessary to bring the provinces in one by one-these were his own words. He said that it was quite a task to bring in the representatives of the nine provinces to achieve the adoption of an agreement. I would take the minister's mind and the minds of his colleagues back to the days before the last election when the Prime Minister told the country that there was one hope for Canada and that was that, there being eight provinces with Liberal governments, if the people would put in a Liberal government they would have liberalism marching down the corridors of democracy to a revival of good times. Well, the government has been in power over two and a half years. I remember telling some of the new members in the first speech I made in this parliament, two years ago last January, that the Liberal party had the most wonderful opportunity to lead Canada out of its distress-a marvellous opportunity. But I did warn them of this: 1 said that there were certain things peculiar to the politics of Canada, among them being that insidious thing called patronage, which I feared greatly would obtrude its head from time to time and prevent the Liberal party from achieving its great destiny. How have my hon friends taken advantage of their opportunities?
I have before me statements made by Premier Hepburn a few days ago, and they are similar to many statements that have been made. I do not agree with him in all his policies, but I will say this about him. He is a young man, a Liberal; he is vigorous in the administration of his government; he may be doing things that some of us do not like, but he is a strong leader of a strong Liberal government in the biggest province in Canada. And there is no unity between the minister and that province-no unity. Who is responsible for that lack of unity? I do not know. It is not my duty to say, but I will say that there is a lack of unity between the Liberal government at Ottawa and the Libera] government in Ontario.
Then I turn to the great province of Quebec. The government in office there is not a Liberal government, it is true; but I ask the minister: Why the other day, as was indicated in a speech by the premier of
(Mr. Stevens.]
Quebec, would he refuse to meet the mayor or representatives from the city of Montreal in regard to a great practical scheme to deal with unemployment?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend wish
the answer?

I expected the minister
to make an answer of that kind. I find here, in his own measure introduced two years ago, the dominating measure indicating the government's policy with respect to unemployment in Canada, one purpose was to:
recommend to the minister measures with respect to programs of public works and projects of the dominion, the provinces, the municipalities and other agencies. . . .

Through the provinces,

No, it does not. What it says is this, that if and when unemployment insurance is established, and a national employment service set up across the country, then there should be a national system of unemployment aid. If my hon. friend knows as much about the relief situation as he purports to do, he must know that at the present time relief covers the unemploj'ed and the unemployable. There is no suggestion in

Relief and Agricultural Distress
the report from beginning to end that the dominion government should take over relief one hundred per cent at the present time.

speechtext: I did not say relief.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I said that the recommendation of the commission was that the dominion government should take over responsibility for unemployment, and it is true that they did reserve to the municipalities that portion of relief which existed before the depression, such as sickness, indigency and so on. No one considers that as part of this program at all. It is like the poor of whom the good book speaks; there are a certain number of poor unfortunate people whom we have always with us.
The report certainly recommends that this parliament should take control of industrial unemployment, ""he minister, in the face of that recommendation, fixes himself firmly in this position, that he will do nothing with a municipality, no matter how important it may be, how large it may be, or how precise and definite may be its proposals, unless it comes to him through the provincial government. All right, let him take that position; one of the reasons why this whole problem hangs over Canada to-day is this quibbling about constitutional jurisdiction, this habit of "passing the buck," this quibbling about whether a particular officer of this particular government shall talk to another particular officer or not. Let us sweep aside these silly, incompetent administrative practices and face the issues frankly. If the city of Montreal is prepared to pay 83,000,000 and the province of Quebec is prepared to pay 83,000,000 towards a project, let this government definitely say yes or no to the project, and not quibble about these other matters.
But I disagree with the idea of the dominion government and the dominion parliament taking the responsibility, because in my opinion the whole question narrows itself down to one of economics and not to a dispute about constitutional authority. The economics are extremely simple. The municipalities are calmly told by the dominion, and sometimes by the province, that theirs is the responsibility. We, the dominion parliament and government, say: We shall be glad to render a certain amount of aid in the form of charitable contributions, but we insist that the responsibility is yours. At the same time we deny the municipalities and the provinces an opportunity to get sufficient revenue to
discharge these obligations. There is not a city in Canada to-day that is not bankrupt or going bankrupt.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Go easy; that is not true as to Sherbrooke.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Well, I will say this for the benefit of my hon. friend, that as far as I know there is scarcely a city in Canada except Sherbrooke that is not either bankrupt or on the verge of bankruptcy. Why? Because of the intolerable burden of relief. Municipal taxes are raised to the point where building cannot go on, where real estate is dead, where the whole machinery of construction and building and housing is blocked because of the unholy height of municipal taxes. Yet we stand here, not only offering no assistance, but calmly telling the municipalities that theirs, is the responsibility; that they must discharge that duty, and at the same time we deny them a chance to get a fair amount of revenue to carry out that responsibility.
The suggestion of the employment commission that certain phases of their duties cannot be discharged because the government has appointed another commission on the constitutional question is an insult to the intelligence of parliament. Does it mean that we shall quibble along about constitutional difficulties for another year or two, or until after the next general election, before the Rowell commission reports, when all the time it is not a constitutional difficulty at all but a question of economics? It is a question of taxation and of revenue. What we should have done, instead of appointing this commission, was to use the officers that we have in the employ of the government, men like Doctor Coats, Mr. Sim, Mr. Fraser Elliott, the head of the income tax branch, Mr. Sellar-I could name a dozen outstanding experts.

speechtext: They are Tories.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: No; they are not-well, I have no knowledge whatever of the politics of any of these men.

others-are men unexcelled in the United States or any other country for their ability to find the solution of Canadian problems.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Why did the hon. member not do it?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I did as far as I was able. Let me give my hon. friend an experience I had which warrants me in making that statement. There was brought before me as Minister of Trade and Commerce a question regarding a conflict between the accountancy systems of the provinces and the dominion in, computing the tax for income and other purposes. So I asked Doctor Coats to call in the deputy ministers of the treasury departments of the provinces. We brought them here. I presided at the first meeting. I said, "Now gentlemen, this is a technical question in accountancy;" and I presented the problem to them. I left them to deal with it; they worked it out in about a week, and from that day to this there has been complete harmony in that extremely technical realm between the provinces and the dominion.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: That was done under Doctor Coats.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Certainly, at my instance. I presided over the first meeting.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: And I think it was a very good thing.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
And exactly the same thing could be done now. When I suggest that these outstanding civil servants should be used, I do so because I have confidence in the civil service of Canada. There are dozens of men, men recognized in other countries as outstanding, who could be used. Let me cite one instance to support what I am saying. Our dominion statistician, Doctor Coats, is recognized in the United States and in every country in Europe as one of the outstanding statisticians in the world. We ought to be proud of him. There are other civil servants who in their spheres are equally competent. These are the men who should be charged with these tasks. Let them call in actuaries, accountants, provincial treasurers, tax experts from the large cities, and go into conference on these technical economic questions of revenue, taxation and the burden of relief upon the provinces and the municipalities, and there would be no more worry about the British North America Act or this passing of responsibility from one body to the other. The problem would be solved on a basis of mathematics and economics. This suggestion is, I think, worthy of consideration, and I ask the minister to reconsider his determined 
view that this is a responsibility solely of the municipalities. It is that thought perpetually advanced which is causing trouble throughout Canada to-day. Unless the municipalities are assisted in getting revenue from other sources than their present limited ones, so that they can lower their taxation on real estate, we shall never get very far with any housing scheme.
Mr. ST-PERE:	That is the problem.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I have in mind the statement of the mayor of Calgary, that the dominion government should take over the entire cost of relief. It is a cry of desperation. He indicated that the city no longer intended to be financially responsible for a situation which was not of its making and which it was impossible for it to correct. We heard from Winnipeg a day or two ago, what it had to do; that it had spent some 810,000,000 in the last two years, and that it had to use its reserves and sinking fund. We know the state of Vancouver-

speechtext: And the same in Toronto.

speechtext: I just want to point out to the hon. gentleman that the Canadian report of cities which was issued last year states just the opposite.

speechtext: All right. All I have to say is this: I know every city in Canada personally; I have looked at them all, and I am expressing my own opinion when I say that our cities to-day, in their downtown sections, are in the main hazards to health as well as being hazards from the standpoint of fire, and ought to be rebuilt. Further, it will take us thirty years to build up our cities and towns to a reasonably decent level of construction. But the minister says that the municipalities are responsible for relief, and that he will deal with them only through the provinces. The minister and his colleagues will have to face this question sooner or later. They have failed to face it in the last two years; they have failed utterly to face it through this commission, because this report does not contain anything in that connection except some pious observations that we ought to have a housing scheme; that we ought to have unemployment insurance, and that we ought to encourage the tourists. Is there anything new about that? What about the tourist branch?

speechtext:
My hon. friend was in
office here for five years. Did he advocate all these things at that time?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: He did; but I would also suggest to the minister that I left office.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I am aware of that.

speechtext:
Certainly I advocated

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: In this house?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
In this house and out
of it. Since 1931 I have consistently taken a strong stand on this question of housing throughout Canada. I am speaking alone in this house; but I would remind the minister that while that is so, and while I can be very easily brushed aside as far as the house is concerned, I represent 381,000 votes. I am not ashamed of those votes. I am not ashamed of my record, nor am I ashamed of the policies I advocate. I am not ashamed of the policies for which I gave up office. What the minister says is no answer. He can, if he so desires, lay on me, as the last part of his speech indicated he was quite capable of doing, all sorts of political opprobrium, but that will not alter his responsibility one iota. He is the minister. He came to the house with this proposal two years ago, and at the time I warned him that we would hold him and his government responsible for results from this measure. That was two years ago; the results have been nil.
Let me complete what I was saying about housing. It will take us thirty years to catch up in that regard if we do not give the municipalities of this country relief from the burden of the cost of unemployment, either by talcing over the whole responsibility or by giving them new sources of revenue, which we could do very simply and easily. Unless we do something of that kind, there can be no housing, because the municipalities cannot afford to do it and no one is going into a housing scheme with the taxes he has to pay to-day.
The minister referred to the tourist business. Of course the tourist business is good, but the minister just discovered it. He brings it to the house as a new discovery by this commission. They refer to the tourist business ; it is one of their chief accomplishments. Why. Mr. Chairman, for some years we have had within the ambit of the government of Canada a department or a branch of a department dealing with the tourist business. We have been encouraging the tourist business through other departments. I noticed that the minister spoke about the Department of Mines and Resources, the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce. At first I thought the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was delivering the address.

Relief and Agricultural Distress
Usually it is left to the Prime Minister to deal with the affairs of all the departments, but the minister spoke of them quite freely. The Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) has been doing very good work. I have commended him for what he has done in the expansion of mining; but when the Minister of Labour quotes figures showing the increased production of gold as an evidence of what the employment commission did, it is pretty thin. It may be good politics. It may be good stuff as a sort of sedative for dissatisfied Liberal supporters throughout the country. It may be, but I doubt it. But for the minister to suggest to the house that the increase in the production of gold in this country is to be credited to him and to this commission is stretching things pretty far.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: There is no suggestion of that at all. My hon. friend can look up the record.

speechtext: Must I read everything the minister said?

speechtext: That had no connection with the commission at all.

speechtext: I have in my hand a copy of his three hour speech, and in it he gave the increase in gold production.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: That had no reference to the employment commission at all. I was dealing with the expanding trade policies of the government.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Was that not referred to by the employment commission?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I hold in my hand three pages of this report devoted exclusively to the export business. The minister went ahead and quoted the increases in exports. What were those increases? As I said two years ago in my speech on the budget, had there not been hanging over the world threats of war-a condition which unfortunately has not clarified in the last year or two-our exports would have been very much less than they are. An analysis of our exports shows that a very substantial portion of the increase is for that class of export which is involved in the production of armaments. Yet the minister quoted the improvement in exports,
TMr. Stevens.]
the tourist business and the extension of gold production as evidences of a solution of these problems.
The whole question is one of confidence and unity. The whole question is one of leadership by this parliament. I am not now for the moment placing the onus of responsibility in this respect on the government. This parliament-and, by the way, a parliament can express its leadership only through its government

ought to give leadership to industry, leadership to finance and leadership to the provinces in the approach to the solution of this problem.
The question of debt and taxation lies at the root of the whole trouble. This government has heaped opprobrium particularly on the government of Alberta. It has gone out of its way to paint the activities of the Alberta government in every known possible term. Why? Because the premier of Alberta is the exponent of some peculiar ideas in economics, with which, by the way, I do not agree. But he is the premier of Alberta. In this house there now sits a young man who only the other day was returned from the capital city of that province, indicating that the people of Alberta are feeling very keenly and very deeply. What is the root of all the trouble? The awful burden of debt.
Nevertheless there is not a word in this report about that, the root cause, almost the main cause, of dissatisfaction, and of social and political dislocation in Canada. When the farmers of Alberta who, if I remember correctly, number about 500,000, realize that they have to pay eight, nine or ten per cent interest on mortgages on farms; when they realize that they have to pay from ten per cent to thirty per cent interest on deferred payments on agricultural implements-and I can produce a list of two hundred from one district alone-and when they find, after borrowing the money and during ten and, in some instances, twenty years paying more than they borrowed

that at the end of the period they owe more than when they started, then they must ask, "What hope is there for us? Where are we going to get assistance?"
Mr. Aberhart has at least done this:	He
has shown that he is desirous of lifting the burden of debt. His methods and processes may be wrong. I do not agree with the social credit theory; but I do agree with this, that the root cause of the dissatisfaction is the unbearable burden of debt. It may be that in the older provinces that condition may not be realized as keenly as it is in the west.
I wish to make a statement here which I think would warrant careful consideration, and it is this: There is a good deal of talk

Relief and Agricultural Distress
about the losses incurred by eastern financial institutions in western Canada. We hear a great deal about that. I venture this statement, and challenge its contradiction: In the last twenty-five years the farmers of the three western provinces have paid in interest rates in excess of six per cent more than double the total capital or interest lost in those three provinces by mortgage and loan companies. I repeat that, because it lies at the root of our trouble, when we talk about agricultural distress. True, the drought area is the first catastrophe, but it is not the sum total of agricultural distress out there. It is due to debt. I say that these farmers have paid in interest rates in excess of six per cent, which would be a moderate rate, more than double the total losses in principal and interest in the last twenty-five years. These men know that something is wrong, and they are asking for some relief. They are asking us to lift this burden of debt from their shoulders. Parliament may not be clothed with all the responsibility; but unless it gives leadership in the approach to the solution of this problem, there will be no cessation of dissatisfaction in connection with these matters.
So I say to the minister that this report, a major portion of which, by the way, is taken up in a discussion of export trade, and another portion in a discussion of the tourist business, lamentably fails, and the minister in his speech failed to indicate any worth while and practical methods of dealing with this great problem.
Before I take my seat, let me add one further word. I do not know what the minister is going to introduce, and it might be said to me, "You might have waited until the bill came down." But I am taking the proper, parliamentary procedure. This resolution, together with the minister's statement, is supposed to indicate the government's policy on this subject. If the minister has something up his sleeve, and if there is something to be disclosed later on which is much in advance of anything he has indicated or has disclosed in the resolution, then he is not dealing fairly with parliament. I am bound by what I can see and by what the minister has said. I take it for granted that he was honest and honourable, took the committee into his confidence and disclosed the government policy. That is the one and the only thing an honourable man could do. Taking that position, I say to him that I find, not no hope, but little hope for a solution of the problem. I question whether the minister himself is satisfied.
He came to this house a few years ago, a young man highly trained, a young man with an academic training, an economist of note,
a man to whom the country looked as adding youth, virility and vision to the government. But as I listened to his speech the other day I realized that the first half of it was a laboured statement to justify the report, and the last half of it was a disquisition on the record of the government, dealing with every department of it, a speech which might have been delivered by the Prime Minister in connection with a budget, or on some other occasion of that kind. But it was not at all germane to this subject. He left us in a hopeless morass, so far as any solution of this stirring problem is concerned.
It is not good enough to say that we have supplied some means of training youth and to leave the underlying problems-and as an educated and cultured man, and a student of economy, he knows these problems exist- behind the dark screen. Either he did not have the courage or he was not allowed to disclose them. I think myself he would, had he been allowed, have brought them to the light of day. But he did not.
One point further, and it is this:	It is
rumoured that the government proposes to introduce a long list of public works, to be scattered throughout the various constituencies, as a contribution toward the solution of this problem. If that is done, all I can say is that it is an indication that an election is in the offing. That is no contribution toward the solution of the problem, and if it is contemplated I would plead with the government to abandon it. We shall see when it comes; we can only guess. But if it does come, I warn the minister it will be looked upon in that light. From what we are able to learn, there is little hope given to the unemployed; there is little hope given to the struggling manufacturer; there is little hope given to the distressed agriculturist.
