I deplore very much
indeed that this condition two years afterwards is the answer to the very bright speech which the minister made two years ago when he introduced the bill upon which this commission was founded.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speech just made by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens). It is needless for me to say that he was not looking at me when he said that this country was looking to parliament for leadership. I am a Leader by name only; yet I am proud of my name, and I am proud of my occupation as a farmer.

Relief and Agricultural Distress
This debate on unemployment in Canada has been very interesting and instructive. I can think of nothing that affects more deeply the lives of the Canadian people than a solution of this great problem. I am thinking now of the eve of the general election in 1930, when the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), appealing to the people, at that time said that the greatest problem confronting the Canadian people was that of unemployment. "Give me power," he said, "and I' will cure unemployment or perish in the attempt." And in the fortunes of political war he perished in the attempt.
Another government came into power, and after they had been in power for nearly three years we find a responsible minister saying that unemployment is the most vital question affecting the Canadian people. I am making these statements in order to indicate that we have not yet solved this great problem. It will take some years to solve it. It will take the united efforts of all the members of parliament to solve it, and I hope we get that concerted action.
I do not think the problem will be settled by the expansion of our tourist traffic, important as that is. I do not wish to minimize the value of that great trade, but I do not think it goes to the root of the trouble. Nor do I think that youth training is going to solve the problem of unemployment, very necessary as I believe that is, because, Mr. Chairman, what is the use of training young people for certain occupations if you cannot give them a job?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Hear, hear; now you are talking.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I do not believe the setting up of employment agencies will solve unemployment, for the same reason that I gave a moment ago-what is the use of employment agencies if you cannot give the worker a job?
Perhaps my hon. friends sitting opposite do not believe that the expansion of our trade is of so much importance. I believe that it is of vital importance, and that the efforts of the present government have had the effect of developing and expanding our trade so much during the last two years that we have had more or less of a boom in comparison with conditions which obtained previously. I think the trade agreement which this government made with the United States was a wonderful achievement. The right hon. leader of the opposition said that he could have obtained the same trade agreement from the United States had he so desired. If that is so, then I believe the Conservative party
[Mr. Loader.)
were in error in not accepting it, and I want to commend the Liberal government for accepting that trade agreement with the United States. But that has not solved our unemployment problem, and it is the duty of parliament to find a solution for it and to provide the necessary remedy.
When I was elected a member of parliament-and by the way I represent 25,000 people in western Canada, and I am speaking here not in my own interests but in the interests of those who sent me here, and if at any time I express in this house sentiments that are contrary to those I know my people hold, I know I shall have to pay the penalty; I shall be the one to suffer-when I was elected I wanted to give a fair day's work for a fair day's pay, and I wondered what I could do to help solve the problems of Canada. Being a very humble member of parliament, but knowing the agricultural situation, and knowing that great numbers of agricultural workers throughout the country were unemployed and had drifted into our cities, I investigated the farm placement plan which had been adopted by the previous government. I felt that the administration of the plan had not gone far enough. I believed in the plan, but I thought that something more could be done.
I am not giving away any secrets, although perhaps I am giving information when I say that the farm placement plan was first suggested to the former government by the deputy minister of labour of Manitoba, Mr. MacNamara, but I want to give them credit for adopting the plan. The plan was for the federal government to pay the agricultural worker five dollars a month and another five dollars a month to the farmer for whom he was working. But after a few months the former government ceased to pay anything to the farmers and carried out only that part of the plan providing for the payment of five dollars a month to the agricultural worker. If the government is going to get credit for instituting the plan, it must also take the responsibility for making it a partial failure. I felt that if we could give these farmers, who were in dire need at that time, ten dollars a month to board these men, we could extend the plan and take in thousands more of these unemployed single men in our cities, and so I got busy. At the first public opportunity I took the matter up with the United Farmers of Manitoba, who were holding their annual convention in the city of Portage la Prairie that year. I discussed the plan at their meeting and presented a resolution asking them to endorse a policy whereby the dominion

Relief and Agricultural Distress
government would put the plan into effect, and the resolution passed unanimously. I came to Ottawa and submitted the plan to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), he discussed it in the house, and the plan eventually was adopted.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Yes. Yesterday the hon. member for Greenwood, (Mr. Massey) gave credit to the late government for instituting the plan, which statement I have corroborated, but I have added that the late government must take responsibility for making just half a job of it. I have told the committee of the procedure I followed in introducing that measure into the house; I am now going to read the words of the minister himself, and I do not think he will deny me that right. Speaking in this house on April 9, 1937, he is reported at page 2824 of Hansard as follows:
Mr. Rogers: I should like to say here, and I am glad of this opportunity to do so, that during the discussion of unemployment arid relief a year ago the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) brought to the attention of the house the importance of enabling single unemployed men in the cities to go to the farms, particularly during the winter months, and also the advantage to the farmers of having that additional assistance during this period.
The hon. member made a definite proposal, as I recall it, which has been largely carried out in the actual farm employment plan which has been in operation. I give that simply as one illustration to assure hon. members that those responsible for particular departments frequently profit, and ought to profit, from the suggestions which come to them from various quarters of the house.
I would add that a government should profit by opinions expressed on all sides, and should take heed to them. I think the government, in giving credit to an hon. member who happens to be a friend of the administration, should be glad that its supporters are in a position sometimes to offer constructive criticisms. Honest criticism coming from a friend should it seems to me, be regarded as perhaps the best advice possible.
I am sure that had the hon. member for Greenwood known the facts, he would not have made the statement he did make yesterday.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: What statement?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I shall read it. The hon. member was discussing the farm placement plan, and he said:
It was with some degree of satisfaction that the minister reported what had been done under the farm improvement, employment and settlement plan. The minister realizes, as does the national employment commission, that 51952-134
this plan was not set up by this government, not even recommended by the national employment commission, but constituted by the former government. The present government has to its credit, let it be said, the fact that it adopted the principle of that plan.
Mr. Martin: Look at the difference in the results.
Mr. Massey: I have noted them. The plan under the former government was and still is a great success, but do not forget the origin and point from which it started, and give credit where credit is due. Fifty thousand men have been placed under the scheme and the minister is to be congratulated upon having accepted it. Surely the government and the national employment commission should not assume any credit for this plan.
The hon. member was not in the chamber when I told the committee that Mr. MacNamara, deputy minister of labour of Manitoba, suggested the plan to the former government. I gave that government credit for adopting the plan, but I also censured them because they discontinued the bonus of five dollars a month to the farmer. That proposition was brought into the house by myself; only I suggested ten dollars a month to both the farmer and the farm hand.
I was going on to say that I am sure the hon. member for Greenwood did not know that those are the actual facts or he would not have arrogated to himself the duty of claiming this credit for the former government.
That the government has accepted the plan which was suggested gives me encouragement and prompts me to offer another. The plan I am about to mention has been alluded to previously in this chamber. It has to do with that part of the report which deals with the rehabilitation of agriculture. During the campaign I had occasion to speak over the radio, and I prepared a fifteen minute talk on how to rehabilitate agriculture, how we cotffJ devise some scheme to keep our people on the land, rather than have them drift to the cities. I have the statement before me. I am going to read but very little of it, as I wish to hasten on with my remarks. I told the people of the money that was being spent at that time. I believe the then leader of the opposition stated that over three hundred million dollars had been expended in unemployment relief, and that nothing of a concrete nature had been devised. I spoke of great public buildings which had been erected throughout the dominion at a huge cost to the taxpayers, not a dollar of the expense having been paid in cash, every dollar being borrowed money on which interest would have to be paid in perpetuity. I told them of the relief camps and what they were doing to the nation. By the way, before I get away



Relief and Agricultural Distress
from that point let me state, what perhaps I should have mentioned a few moments ago, that the adoption of the farm placement plan had the effect of closing those camps. Last year, I believe, over fifty thousand workers, men and women, were placed on farms, at a cost of something over three and a half million dollars to the taxpayers. The last year the relief camps were in operation, according to figures which, I understand, were given by the minister, the cost was in the neighbourhood of nine million dollars, and the prospective expense for the following year was twelve million dollars. But under the farm placement plan we were able to close the relief camps and reduce our cost by two-thirds.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Were as many men taken care of?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Yes, far more. On an average there were, I believe, only twenty thousand in the relief camps, whereas last year fifty thousand men and women were placed on farms. I said in my address that the handling of the relief at that time was more or less of a political nature, because there was no employment commission, there was no real foundation on which the government could work, and many decisions were made at a time when matters did not receive mature judgment owing to the emergency, with the result that the work and the appointments were more or less political. Then I told them of the plan of the leader of the opposition at that time:
The alternative method of handling the unemployment problem is found in the platform of the Liberal party as outlined by Mackenzie King. Mr. King and his followers pledge themselves to appoint a National Unemployment Commission which will represent all parts of Canada, all classes of society, and all interests of the community. That body will be nonpolitical. It will be in a position to consider each relief project strictly upon its merits and to advise the government accordingly.
The commission was duly appointed. Perhaps all hon. members will not believe that it has accomplished much, but if it has not, this certainly was not the fault of the commission. I went on to outline a plan by which we could help the unemployed and keep our people on the land. We have heard from all parts of the chamber suggestions by hon. members as to electrical energy being placed at the disposal of the fanning population. I do not know of any farmers in the west, unless perhaps there are a dozen or so around my city of Portage la Prairie, who enjoy the use of electrical energy in their farm homes. I believe it is for lack of this facility more than anything else that young people are 
leaving our farms. Men, and women, boys and girls, are going to the cities. They see the conveniences there, and are discouraged when they return home and realize what they have to put up with. This, we are told, is a machine age. It is true that farmers have a great deal of machinery to help them in their work; but farm women are without the devices which are at the disposal of city women, and so the younger generation tend to drift towards the cities because they have no pride in their occupation and no heart in their work. So I suggested this:
We all know, and no one better than those who are engaged in farm work, that farm life is not so attractive as city life. Farm houses generally lack the modern convenience found so universally in the city. Although Canada has an abundance of electrical energy generated to meet the requirements of all citizens, our governments have not yet been able to place this power within the reach of the farmer's pocket-book. This is one reason why our young farmers, both boys and girls, prefer a doubtful existence in the city to the more permanent though humdrum life on the farm. These young people should be retained on the land otherwise they will displace workers in the city. This could be done in a large measure if our governing bodies would undertake to supply farmers with electrical energy and not limit the benefits of this modern laboursaving device to those residing in our towns and cities. Why, and it is a pertinent question, should not farm women have the same opportunities as their sisters in the city and simply by the pressing of an electric button be relieved of much of the drudgery of housekeeping?
Then I told them that I knew from personal observation and through contact of thousands of retired farmers or farmers who had lost their farms and who were living in our cities on relief. I said that those farmers would give their right arm to get back to the old farm again, but that there was no opportunity for them. I told them of farm workers who had laboured for years and years on the farm, but who, owing to the depression, could not go back with any chance of getting a job. I told them about the returned soldiers, and perhaps I should read the paragraph dealing with this class:
Then, too, the returned soldier, who offered his all for the welfare of the nation should be taken care of. Perhaps he and his family would like to be reestablished on good land in a good district. The fact that he had failed in a previous experience should be no detriment. Perhaps our government was greatly to blame for his failure because we know that many of these men were placed where they had no chance to succeed owing to having started on poor land in a poor district and with expensive equipment. I know of many returned men who are separated from their

Relief and Agricultural Distress
families by force of circumstances that would welcome the chance to reestablish their homes on the land, had they an opportunity.
I am thinking now of one incident in particular that occurred while I was loading a car of wheat at a siding at Burnside. There was a man of perhaps forty years of age who was working for another farmer, and he said to me, "My wife and two children are back home living with her father and mother. We were placed on a farm and were anxious to succeed. But after a year or two we came to the conclusion that no man in Canada could make a living on it." Consequently they abandoned the farm and his wife and two children went back home, while he became a hired man. There are thousands of such cases, and the minister himself told us that many of these soldiers have not had a fair chance to succeed.
I should like to read the plan that I submitted then. Here it is:
Now I think that the Canadian government should undertake at the earliest possible moment to place these ex-farmers and the others that I have mentioned back on the land. They could be located on much of the land that is at present a burden to the resident farmer.
What I meant by being a burden to the resident farmer was this: In my own district of Portage la Prairie, I know of fathers who are themselves the sons of old pioneers who went there from Ontario and Quebec. They are now seventy years of age with four or five sons, not one of whom is at home. Where are they? They have gone to the cities, either in Canada or in the United States, to find employment. They would like nothing better than to take up a quarter section or half a section of the land belonging to their fathers, but they have not the means. The father, perhaps, has a big mortgage, or a small mortgage it may be, on the farm and he cannot get hold of any money for the purpose of establishing a son on a farm across the road. Consequently the son leaves home and goes to the city. And by the way, when the boys leave home it is a natural consequence that the farm girls do likewise. Therefore, it should be, and, in fact, it is the duty of the government-and I believe they recognize it-to try to keep these farmers' sons and daughters on the land where they were bom. To continue:
In my opinion the federal government should undertake to finance this scheme. Money can be procured at the present time at a very low rate of interest. It could be loaned to the provinces who in turn would deal through the municipalities whose councillors would be in the best position to judge, not only the quality of the land but after investigation the capabilities of the land-seeker.
I believe the minister will discover some similarity between some of the recommendations contained in the report and what I have been reading to the committee.
In proposing that the federal, provincial and municipal governments should cooperate in the operation of this scheme I am endorsing the policy of the Liberal party as outlined in Mr. King's radio address in which he advocates unity of purpose if we are to achieve beneficial and permanent results. Furthermore, the plan could be carried out with a minimum of expense as it would not be necessary to engage a staff of government officials to add to our burden of taxation.
That could be done by our municipalities without costing the taxpayers one cent, and I believe it is what the report recommends. I believe that is the system which is recommended for adoption by federal, provincial and municipal governments. I do not know whether the farm loan board would take care of a matter of this kind, but it seems to me that is the agency through which we might work. The present farm loan legislation is, in my opinion, a mere pretence.

speechtext: A waste of good paper.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
It does not go far enough. In my opinion, the farm loan board's operations could be extended so as to enable it to buy a lot of this land from farmers who have now more than they can work economically. The result would be that the farmers' sons could apply to the board for a loan on some of the land. This money could be paid to the father who owns the land, and his son would be established. In this way two purposes would be served at the same time. The aged farmer would not sit down waiting for the old age pension; he would be relieved of his mortgage on the old homestead and would be quite content to live there the rest of his days looking across the fence or over the roadway and watching the progress of his son, happily married, carrying on the traditions of his forefathers.
I submit that our system has been all wrong. I do not think one dollar should be paid out in direct relief. All moneys paid out should go to men who work, unless they are unemployable, in which event they are the subjects of charity and we should look after them. I have here some figures given by the Hon. Mr. Garson, provincial treasurer of Manitoba. In the last five years there has been paid out in that province-I believe these are the total figures for the dominion and the province-for direct family relief, including the drought areas, the sum of 835,604,730.19. At the same time they paid
The Royal Assent

out $818,699.12 for rural rehabilitation. In other words, they paid out over S40 for direct relief for which we get no benefit and from which we have no chance of ever getting a return, to only SI spent for reestablishing our people on the land. That is the situation in Manitoba. That is why the minister mildly condemns the plan of rehabilitation which we have had up to the present time. The minister said, in answer to a question of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps), that capital expenditure should not be undertaken unless it provides national income. To that I most heartily agree. But if there is anything which will bring in national income and produce a better morale in this country, or any other country for that matter, it is having a happy, contented rural population.

The house resumed consideration in committee of the following proposed resolution- Mr. Rogers-Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

maintopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I
was saying when the committee rose at six o'clock, most of the people in the southern end of the townships of East York and Scarborough and the southern portion of North York moved out to those municipalities between the years 1916 and 1929, and built what at that time were termed "shacks." Most of these people worked in the building trades in Toronto during the day time and they built their houses in the evening. When 1929 came, most of them had fairly good working men's houses erected, and when they fell out of work they had no reserve. All they had left was their little home.
I want to give the committee some figures to show to the minister that the statement of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) this afternoon to the effect that most of the municipalities in this country are bankrupt had a good deal of truth in it. I will give figures of the assessment, the levies, the arrears of taxes, the property taken over already and the property that is expected to be taken over by these municipalities in the year 1938.
In the township of East York we have an assessment of S14,497,000; the levy is $1,085,000, and the arrears of taxes, $1,040,000, or almost equal to one year's total tax levy. The property that has already been taken over by the municipality amounts to $325,244, and let me say to the minister that every time a piece of property is taken over by the municipality, no further taxes can be collected on it and the rest of the property owners must bear that extra burden. Properties on the tax roll that are expected to be taken over in East York in 1938 amount to $160,000.
In North York the assessment is $10,685,000; the levy, $670,000; arrears of taxes, $495,000; property taken over, $119,901, and the property that is expected to be taken over in the year 1938 amounts to $244,674.
In the township of Scarborough the assessment is $10,475,000; the levy, $620,000, arrears of taxes, exactly half a million dollars. I hesitate to give figures of the property that has been taken over by the municipality, but I have here a publication which has been prepared by the county of York, and it shows that this municipality has taken over $1,584,000 of property; those are the actual tax arrears owing on the property-not the assessment.
What is going to happen to these municipalities in another few years if they continue to take over property at this rate? It will mean that before very long the biggest part of this assessment will be owned by the municipality, and what are the other property owners going to do then? The municipality has paid interest on debenture debt at the rate of 3 per cent, but it has paid no principal since 1933.
In 1928 the township of East York had a building program of $2,600,000; in 1937 it had a building program of $360,000. The bill for relief for the month of January of this year was $53,138; for February, $57,477; and for March just closed, $58,802, of which the municipality is asked to pay approximately $12,000 a month. The number of those on relief in the month of January was 5,523, and in February, 5,977.
One big drawback that we have in these municipalities is that we have no factories. There are no industries of any kind, and consequently all the taxes have to be levied on the homes, which constitute the only property available for taxation. The school tax in some instances amounts to 50 per cent of the total tax levied, and in most instances the school tax, plus the relief tax, amounts to more than 50 per cent and in some instances to 60 or 65 per cent of the total tax levied.
The	minister	may	say	that there	is nomoney	to	look	after	this	situation.	But Iwould point out that from 1935, the last year the Conservatives were in power, until this year the revenues of this country have increased by some $93,000,000, and if the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) went down to my riding and attempted to make a speech there,	the	first	thing he	would be	askedwould	be:	What are	you	going to	do for
Relief and Agricultural Distress

the unemployed? If he told them that there was no money, they would say: There is plenty of money for Saskatchewan; there is plenty of money for defence, plenty of money to pay the deficits on the Canadian National Railways, and plenty of money to pay the interest on the bonds of the Dominion of Canada.
I want to give a few instances of men who have lost their property. One is the case of a gentleman who had given thirty-five years of his life to the public service of the municipality as school trustee, reeve, member of the county council, and so on. The five acres that he owned had been in his family for sixty years. Four years after he died his property was taken over by the municipality for arrears of taxes, and the rest of his family have not a dollar to live on. What is going to happen to them I do not know.
Another family have lived on their farm for 125 years, and cleared the bush off their farm originally. This property has been taken over by the municipality, and what is going to happen to the family nobody knows.
Another case I shall cite is that of a returned soldier. He built his own house, and when it was finished he and a number of other returned soldiers built a veterans' hall in the community. The municipality got into financial difficulties, and this man, who happened to be working for the municipality at that time, was laid off, his work being done by relief labour. He had a small mortgage on his home, and the mortgagee came to foreclose the mortgage, but a group of sympathetic friends rallied around the owner and prevented the bailiff from carrying out his orders, and so the man's home for the time being was left alone. The last time I saw him he stated that before he would be put out of his house-and that is the only thing he has left in this world-there would be murder. Whether that would happen I do not know. But I say that one of the reasons why we have what we call "reds" in this country, one of the reasons why this great scam of communism is over Canada, is the injustices that have been done to families along the line that I have indicated. I ask the minister, If he had worked all his life; if all he had left as a result of his work was his house, and if someone came along and took it from him because of a paltry seven or eight hundred dollar mortgage, taxes and interest, what would he do? Yet in the township of East York alone, five hundred people have lost their homes in this way. I do not know where it is all going to end, but conditions are extremely serious.

When the mayors and reeves visited Ottawa a few days ago I understood, from talking to one of them, that they were returning home with a good deal of hope. They expected the minister was going to do something for their relief problem. They said that Premier Hepburn of Ontario was prepared to do his share if the federal government would do theirs, and they gave me to understand that they were assured by the minister that something would be done. If the premier of Ontario is ready to do his share, I do not see why this government should not do theirs. I trust that before the session is over, the minister will do something for these municipalities, for they are in very bad shape financially.

maintopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I listened with deep interest to
the Minister of Labour's magnificent survey of the unemployment situation, in the course of which he stated that the government is seriously contemplating a new plan designed to stimulate the building of low-cost dwellings. So far, it is well known, the wageearning classes have been unable to take advantage of the Dominion Housing Act. May I be permitted to suggest to the minister a low cost housing plan which, in my humble opinion, would be within the reach of the labouring classes?
There is no doubt that the best solution of the unemployment problem lies in the construction of low cost working men's dwellings. Such a project, carried out on a large scale, would furnish considerable employment to labourers, carpenters, masons, bricklayers, plasterers, painters, etc., and also stimulate the building material industries. But there is only one way, in my opinion, to make such a plan practicable, and that is to construct dwellings at such a low cost that every wage-earner may own one by writing off his investment through a moderate monthly payment in the form of rent. To my mind the most practical way to ensure this is to adopt a system along the lines followed in Sweden, Norway and Italy, which consists in creating in the larger municipalities a local commission composed of an architect, a sociologist, and a secretary, who would give their services without remuneration. Such a commission would have a town planner draw up a governing plan of the area in which the municipality is situate. This plan, which would have to be approved by the proper authorities, would indicate the various sites suited to a development comprising groups of fifty to one hundred standardized houses costing no more than S2,400 each. I believe it would be possible

Relief and Agricultural Distress
to get down to this price by building a large number of houses at one time, thus effecting a saving on materials and transportation, and on other costs.
Such a commission, which would be under the control of both the municipality and the federal government but whose activities would be subject to the approval of a central advisory commission located at Ottawa, would, after drawing up the governing plan and making the cadestral subdivisions required for the construction of these houses, select from among the working men of the locality those to whom, after inquiry, it saw fit to assign a building lot, and after having thus distributed the lots among fifty or one hundred persons, would itself undertake the mass construction of the houses. I am convinced that, provided the commission selects working men in employment, a monthly payment of fifteen to twenty dollars would ensure the repayment within fifteen years of the cost of both land and building. The wage-earner will thus find his house fully paid with very little sacrifice on his part.
In order to attain this objective, two things are essential: mass production and a monthly payment of not more than twenty dollars. The existing act is useless to those who do not have a piece of land and some money; it is beyond the reaph of the small wage-earner. Contrary to what has been said, it does nothing to improve living conditions among small urban wage-earners.
The government could lend the required funds, without interest, to the municipalities, which would guarantee the repayment thereof. The local committees and the municipalities could undertake the collection of the sums due, which, as they are collected from the house owners, would be immediately forwarded to the finance department at Ottawa or to the federal commission charged with the administration of the project. I believe that by lending to each Canadian municipality from $100,000 to $5,000,000 or even more, according to size, the government would solve in the soundest way possible the unemployment problem, while providing the country with a tremendously valuable asset and increasing municipal revenues by the surplus wealth thus created.
I would suggest that the government lend $100,000,000 to the municipalities for this purpose. I shall probably be asked where the government is to obtain this money which it will loan without interest to the municipalities. Here is my answer. Have the Bank of Canada issue $100,000,000 of paper money. St. James Street will say that is inflation. I say
it is not; for the $100,000,000 of paper money thus issued by the Bank of Canada will be automatically refunded over a given period, say fifteen years, by the redemption fund constituted by the monthly payments made by the house owners. After a certain number of years, the Bank of Canada will have recovered all the paper money thus issued, which it will destroy as it comes in. In this way the bank will not lose one cent, and the government of Canada will add to the assets of the country and increase the resources of every municipality by providing new taxable property. Moreover, the $100,000,000 which is thus placed in circulation and which would become bank deposits, would place borrowing facilities at the disposal of commerce and industry. The stimulus given to all the building trades would attenuate the economic recession which is becoming more and more apparent and solve the unemployment problem pending a revival of business.
Let us see who are those who will object to such a policy. There are in the first place the banks, which would rather see the government make issues of bonds to which they could subscribe and, without trouble or risk, make a profit consisting of the difference between the interest which they pay to their depositors and that which the government pays them on its bonds. But all the money which the banks invest in government bonds is money withheld from commercial and industrial development. In the second place, there are the small investors, the holders of savings accounts, who may fear that their dollar will lose its purchasing power. To them I say that they are mistaken; for this operation of the Bank of Canada will be only a temporary one designed to create wealth, to provide work and to make money circulate. When it shall have been entirely refunded to the Bank of Canada, the dollar will have lost none of its value, as the situation will be the same as before the $100,000,000 was issued.
Besides, identical operations have been carried out in Sweden and Norway with no effect whatever upon the monetary unit. It must not be overlooked that this expenditure of $100,000,000 will not only provide needed employment and solve the slum problem which is daily becoming more serious in our cities, but also create a permanent national asset.
Such a policy seems to me to be the soundest possible. I find on page 101 of the national employment commission's report, under item (iii):
The employment created by such housing projects will be greater and more widely spread than that afforded by large scale public works.

Relief and Agricultural Distress
Public works, in most cases, are non-productive, whereas working men's dwellings, if built according to the plan that I have just indicated, will assuredly be paid for. Besides, should an owner fail to meet his payments, what is to prevent the municipality from taking over the property and keeping the amount already paid on it? Moreover, a $2,400 house is always salable, and the possibilities of loss, taking into account the payments already effected, are practically non-existent.
I might add that the action I am asking the Bank of Canada to take is not out of line with the bank's practice. In fact, when it increases the price to be paid for gold, it issues paper money and practises inflation. By so doing, it is following the example of the United States government.
I consider it sounder policy to create in this country an asset, which, while increasing Canada's wealth, will solve a pressing social problem and allow our working classes to live a little more comfortably than to augment the gold reserves concentrated in the Bank of Canada's vaults.
The policy that I am now urging upon the government is already being followed by some manufacturers. At St. Gregoire de Montmorency, in my constituency, the Dominion Textile Company employs 2,000 workers. During the first year following my election as representative of these working people, for whom I feel so deeply, I asked the Dominion Textile Company to adopt such a policy, but my appeal brought no result.
The working people of this small town in my constituency live in small houses where, in some instances, three or four families are crowded together. They would be delighted if the government were to adopt a policy such as I have outlined, which would give to each worker his little home and a garden.
In order to solve the social problems which confront us to-day, it is of vital importance that the working man be able to live under conditions which permit him to have, as other social classes have, a home of his own with space around it, where he can breathe freely, and where the sun can penetrate into every room. It is important that he be able to say to his children: I live in a country where it is good to live.
That man, living in such conditions, will hold fast to our national traditions, will cherish all the more the liberty that is ours and will, in such a state of mind, constitute our strongest bulwark against any subversive ideas that may seek to permeate his home.

The present living conditions of our city workers are untenable. It is essential to wipe out the slums in which the working man considers himself an outcast and where his surroundings make him curse the differences which unfortunately exist between men endowed with the same heart, with the same soul.
When selfish industrialists and greedy capital shirk their obligations, it is the duty of the government to come to the rescue with sound and vigorous legislation. This is what I am now asking the government to do.

maintopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
The resolution before us reads:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide assistance towards the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress, and for such payments out of moneys appropriated by parliament as may be necessary for all or any of the purposes of the proposed legislation.
One can easily understand the reason for bringing in this measure so far as agricultural distress in the drought areas in the west is concerned, but one can hardly understand the reason for it in relation to the alleviation of unemployment in general.
I wonder if the memory of hon. members is too short to recall the Liberal campaign cries in 1935. I wonder if the general public still remembers the nicely printed cards and flaming bill-boards: "Get off the relief roll; get on the payroll. Vote for us. Get action. King or chaos." Three years have now passed and the poor misguided electorate are still on the relief rolls or on the edge of the payroll. One would think that those responsible for these election cries had some concrete policy in their minds for the relief of unemployment. We have been waiting now for two and a half years for something concrete from this government elected on these promises, and now we are handed a report of a commission!
The three or four hour speech made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) was void of any immediate hope for the unemployed. No reasons for unemployment were given. The minister attempted to take credit on behalf of the government for such increase in employment as has taken place. Very little that this government has done has improved employment in this country. The improvement which started in the regime of the Conservative government has continued in spite of this government.
If a business gets into difficulties a concrete policy for betterment must be formed without delay. The board of directors must take action to get the business out of its diffi-

Relief and Agricultural Distress
culties. The shareholders will not allow them to "pass the buck" to some other independent body; the responsibility is theirs. The board of directors call in the heads of the various departments and the experts whom they have at their disposal in an endeavour to clear up the difficulties. They go to work step by step; they do not rush in with some theoretical panacea of foreign trade or such cure-alls and then wait for two and a half years for some outside body to report. If they did so, by that time they would have no business. They recognize that maladjustments must be discovered and corrected step by step. That is what the former Conservative government did. First of all they reestablished the Canadian home market. But the constructive program initiated by that government is well on its way to being wrecked by such action as has been taken by the present government.
Every phase of Canadian unemployment cannot be corrected at once. Canada is a young country. Canada was built up nationally. The forefathers of this country made sacrifices for the privilege of living under the British flag and under British laws and traditions, and to be a nation. The whole plant of Canada-our canals, our roads, our railroads, our water powers, our factories, and now our airways and radio-was built with this object in view. Our forefathers were for Canada first, and they expected us to follow that principle. Our national resources should be for the benefit of Canadians, not only those now living but future Canadians. Our forefathers saw the great possibilities and the potential wealth of this country, and we must recognize these facts if we are to have continued prosperity and economic security in this country. We must use our national plant and our national resources for the benefit of Canadians.
We have to go a step further, and recognize the advantages of empire nationalism. The commonwealth is held together by ties which were recognized by our forefathers. These ties were responsible for creating Canada as a nation in the commonwealth; these ties were responsible for the building up of the commonwealth. It is right and proper that we should recognize the advantages of using our national plant and national resources for the benefit of the empire and of the British Commonwealth of Nations. Now that the whole world has gone national, it is ridiculous to think that a little country like Canada can hope to survive by sacrificing our home markets and Canadian industries for unstable markets in countries where these ties do not exist.
The government of the day are entrusted with our natural resources; they are trustees
of the Canadian market for Canadians. But they have been remiss in their trust. Has Canada's board of directors followed a businesslike course? No. The people expected them to act in a businesslike manner. In the 1935 election, bill-boards and election cards cried out, "Get off the relief roll; get on the payroll; vote Liberal; elect us, you will have action!" When the Liberal party was elected and a new cabinet formed, this new board of directors should have directed all their efforts to constructive action. They should have utilized the machinery, such as the bureau of statistics and their experts, to the fullest, extent. They might have utilized their elected members of parliament; but they did not; they set up a commission, which has cost the country two or three hundred thousand dollars. The government passed the buck, they have refused responsibility.
The least I can do is to do something better than the government has done. I wish to make a plea for national unity in the correction of unemployment. The policy of this government, rather than fostering national unity, has to a large extent created disunity. We have discord between one section of the country and another, between classes of labour, between labour and capital, between provincial governments and the federal government. They all have a chip on their shoulder, due to the actions of this government. People in one section of the country are led to believe that prosperity built up in another part of the country, is responsible for the privation and distress of their own section. Banks are blamed; railways are blamed; labour unions are blamed; the weather is blamed for unemployment; but the real blame lies at the door of this government. The people should be brought to realize that prosperity in one part of Canada does not make Canada prosperous; that there is very little chance of one section of the country being prosperous while other parts suffer poverty and distress.
One great difficulty is the enormous increase in federal and provincial debt; another is our tremendous cost of government, resulting in excessive taxation. Everybody wants to work for the government because jobs in industry cannot be had. They are looking for economic security, and that seems to be the only way they can get it. The government must give leadership in the formation of public opinion to correct this overgovernment.
Interest on our enormous public debt must be paid primarily by exports of goods or services which the creditor nations need and must have. No bargaining is necessary here.

Relief and Agricultural Distress
Canada must pay in the equivalent of goods or services; there is no other way. Canada cannot afford to buy from foreign countries any more goods or services than are absolutely necessary, as to do so would still further increase our debt and our foreign obligations, and make unemployment greater. In this country we have everything that is necessary for abundant prosperity if only we had good government leadership. Canadians must have an opportunity for production. We have primary producers of many products which deplete our natural resources, such as pulp, paper, minerals, lumber and so on. We have producers of other products which repeat year after year, such as farm products, wheat, cattle, animal products and so on. We have service products in the tourist trade, the insurance business, the railways and so on. We have secondary producers, who are by far the greatest proportion of the population. Through lack of government leadership and also through unfair propaganda, prejudices have been created. One class of industry is sure that help for another industry will be prejudicial and almost an insult to itself. They want protection for themselves and none for others. In no class of industry can continuity of employment be assured without security to the workers in the other classes. The great fundamental fact is that primarily all the great classes engaged in industry, farmers, doctors, lawyers and everyone, require as much of the home market as they can obtain; the more the better, if we want continuity of employment.
The minister touched on almost every phase of the matter but that which is the most important. Our unemployment urgency requires national unity. That phase of this government's policy with respect to the home market, Canada for Canadians, is the phase on which the minister did not touch. Our unemployment urgency requires national action. It might require sectional sacrifice until such time as a proper balance of employment is arrived at in these various classes of industry. Those who are required to make sectional sacrifices should be properly assisted or compensated; this will be cheaper than the cost of relief for the employable unemployed.
Three years now have passed, and at last we have the report of the national employment commission which was set up in 1936. That commission established a statistical branch and went into action. Clerks, stenographers, secretaries, typewriters, adding machines. tabulating machines and so on all went into action in order that the commission could get the information which they have obtained. They collected statistical
[Mr. Ross (St. Paul's).!
data. This information is useful and illuminating, and it should continue to be collected and tabulated. I think the bureau of statistics, with its trained staff, could do that work without much added expense. The compilation of all this information could have been carried out by that expert branch of the government without any very great increase in cost. Could not the machinery of the bureau have been used for this purpose, without the expenditure of two or three hundred thousand dollars? In any event a great deal of the information obtained was collected by the bureau. The municipalities carried out the registration and collected most of the information. The interim report of the commission was made in July, 1937. The final report was made in January, 1938, and was printed and tabled a few days ago. Why the delay from January to April? Was there difficulty with the report? Or was the report supervised by the government? Or is it an independent report by an independent commission? Surely in view of the gravity of the situation hon. members were entitled to see this report earlier than the month of April, when it was completed in January.
Having regard to the increasingly large number of unemployed, is that action? It is not. We are told that another commission will have to report on the ways and means of carrying out this report. This is action by commission, but it is not action for the benefit of the employable unemployed. As soon as they were elected in 1935 the government took action, observing that general business conditions were steadily improving and that we were recovering from the effects upon the country of the dumping of goods in 1930, due to the policy of the Liberal government of the day. We were recovering rapidly as a result of the Ottawa agreements and the policy of the Conservative government in enforcing dumping duties. This government, hoping that conditions would continue to improve, referred the Employment and Social Insurance Act to the courts. They did not even repeal the act. The hon. member for Temiscouata endeavoured to do so; but as usual this government passed the buck to the courts, spending thousands of dollars of the taxpayers' money in order to have the act declared ultra vires. They did not take steps to see if the provinces would fall in line and agree that necessary steps should be taken to bring this legislation into force. The provinces would have needed little persuasion at that time, but this government refused to approve this legislation, which had been passed by a Conservative government.

Relief and Agricultural Distress
They refused to take action, in spite of their election cry, "Elect a Liberal government and we will be Liberal from coast to coast." Now we know that this cry meant nothing. This act might have been in force to-day with the machineiy running smoothly if there had been action on the part of the government. Anybody with foresight could have seen that under our industrial set-up such legislation was necessary for a great many reasons, and now it has been recommended by the national employment commission, but we must wait for another year or so until we get a report from another commission.
Very little credit can be given the government for the improvement in the unemployment situation, but condemnation may be expressed because of their neglect to conserve the home market for Canadian workers. No one can deny that the dumping of Japanese goods, manufactured under a standard of living which is only a fraction of that enjoyed by our workmen, has taken employment from our workers here. The government refused to stop dumping; no action was taken. Canada has not been prosperous as far as her workmen are concerned. Canada's volume of trade is not the indication of the prosperity of the country. Our prosperity is indicated by the prosperity of the individuals throughout the nation, how much they earn each year, not each day or each week. That means how much work has been done. In three years this government has done nothing to increase the continuity of employment. It has given away the home markets of our secondary industries by not stopping dumping. The depression in the United States which started in October. 1937, has been steadily growing worse. That country had high inventories, which had to be liquidated. For the last four or five months these inventories have been liquidating at the expense of Canadian industry. Almost fifty per cent of our imports from the United States were of finished manufactured articles. Therefore I say that this liquidation has been at the expense of our workers. Our imports from the United States have increased, and our exports to that country have decreased. Our balance of trade with them has become increasingly against us.
What action was taken last October, November or December to stop a continuance of these conditions? Where was the imposition of dumping duties? No action has been taken, and yet the government takes credit for having done good work. It takes credit for placing youth in industry. For years it has been obvious that youth training was necessary. It has also been obvious that when conditions
warranted, manufacturers would encourage that training. They would encourage it when there was a demand for their goods. It is also obvious that government assistance and cooperation were necessary, and I must say that very little credit is due the government for anything which, on the face of it, is so obvious. When conditions warrant, youth training in industry would increase. But what will happen to the trained youth and the old employees? When the demand for manufactured goods declines, the services of employees will have to be dispensed with. I ask this question: What is the use of training the youth if the manufacturers cannot keep them employed? What has the government done to ensure the continued employment of these people?
What is happening at the present time? They are being laid off, or are being told that they will have to work shorter hours. Thousands of young Canadians are reaching the age where they could take work in the industrial fields. What has the government done to ensure work for them? We know it has refused to impose dumping duties on imported goods. Is that the proper action? The work our workmen should do is being done by United States workmen, in order that some purchaser may save a few cents on the dollar. All this is done at the expense of the Canadian workman, and at a heavy relief cost to the government.
Canadian buyers for Canadian firms have orders from their headquarters not to buy. Business houses, because of the policy of the government, are afraid to make purchases. They realize that the government have followed a policy of doing nothing, and that there is uncertainty with respect to the proposed new agreement with the United States. Nobody knows what conditions may be a short time in the future. I know of four industries in Toronto whose business was so good last October that they were cramped for space. Had those conditions continued, they would have built extensions to their plants at a cost of from $10,000 to $40,000. But a Liberal government was in power, and the uncertainty wfith respect to tariffs and proposed new treaties discouraged them from building. They had the idle cash ready to use, but they still have it. They have put up a temporary accommodation at a cost of two or three thousand dollars, and Canadian workmen have been deprived of the work they might have had in the larger extensions.
Those companies are keeping their cash, to tide them through the coming depression- and it is coming. Provincial governments, through legislation, are trying to improve wage
Relief and Agricultural Distress

standards and hours of labour, and these improvements raise production costs. The manufacturer must have protection which protects, or go out of business. Surely he is entitled to a condition whereby he will have fair competition, and protection against dumping. But he knows he will get no action until it is too late. Had action been taken by the government to prevent dumping even as late as last November or December, we would not now be approaching the maelstrom of depression in which the United States now is. Action should be taken right away. Due to the stabilizing effects of the Ottawa agreements passed by the late Conservative government, we might not become involved as deeply as we did in 1930 and 1931. However, if four or five months of dumping takes place, it will take two or three years to recover.
This government is inviting Canada to step into a tail-spin with the United States. In October, November and December, when the indication of recession first became apparent, the urgency for action arose. Was there any action? In the closing months of the last Liberal administration, the early months of 1930, the handwriting of the approaching of the depression was on the wall; but the Liberal government then in power took the same attitude the present government is taking. They had ample warning, and I must add that action is as necessary to-day as it was then.
The condition with respect to employment is getting worse, and something will have to be done. The warning has been given, but there are none so blind as those who will not see. I hope sincerely I am not right in what I cannot help thinking and feeling from the indications, namely, that we are fast approaching another bad depression.
We now have before us the report of the employment commission. An efficient Department of Labour working in cooperation with the minister should have anticipated a great many of these recommendations, and acted upon them. Two and a half years has been lost. There has been a lot of theory, but nothing worth while. To my mind, any atempts which have been made in connection with unemployment, as a result of government action, have had about as much effect as one would bring about by pouring a pail of water into lake Ontario.
Chaos-where did I hear that word? I think the expression " King or chaos " is changing rapidly to " King and chaos." If we do not have proper and constructive action, we shall have much greater chaos than we have to-day.

The people of Canada want work the whole year round. They do not want to work half the year only. Our people want to eat and live decently. Farmers want markets. We know that the best market is the home industrial market, and that the farmer cannot be prosperous unless the industrial worker is prosperous. We must keep our Canadian workmen employed, because relief is repugnant to them. A lack of industrial work means a poor market for the farmer.
This government is doing its best to destroy the home market by refusing to stop dumping into Canada. It is giving work to foreign workmen. It would be better to import the workmen and increase the market for Canadian consumption. By its lack of effective policy in industry it has broken its pledge to the electorate. It has betrayed its trust and shirked its responsibility. The cabinet, the board of directors of the country, should be held responsible for gross negligence in trifling with the livelihood of the workers. It has sacrificed secondary industry for concessions in connection with natural resources. Again I ask this question: Are the workers off the relief rolls and on the payrolls? Have the workers who elected the government been given proper treatment? Those gaily printed cards and flaming billboards should have read: " Get off the payroll and get on the relief roll; King and chaos." The mayors of Ontario are not now making irresponsible threats, as was intimated by the minister a short time ago; they are stating facts.

maintopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is reports like that of the national employment commission which have created a feeling in the minds of the people of Canada that the setting up of commissions is of little value; for in this report we find that no careful analysis has been made of the situation to ascertain the real causes of unemployment. The three hour speech of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) contained no concrete proposals for the abolition of poverty or the settlement of this great problem of unemployment, and I was consequently not surprised to hear that the provincial premiers, particularly the premier of Ontario, were not satisfied with the results of the employment commission. The premier of Ontario said that the speech of the Minister of Labour was a headline and a headache:
Asked if he had any intimation of the nature of Ottawa's relief program, Mr. Hepburn said: " I must confess I am not in the confidence of the government at Ottawa."

Relief and Agricultural Distress
Mr. Hepburn added, "I can't find a concrete program in it, and we are dealing with relief as best we can, having in mind the federal government has withdrawn its support."
Prior to the election the Liberal government promised the people of Canada that if returned to power they would issue money in terms of public need; but now we find that they have curtailed the grants to the provinces, even though many municipalities and provincial governments throughout Canada are bankrupt to-day. We know that these bodies may have their constitutional responsibilities and be responsible for maintaining certain services; They may be responsible constitutionally for maintaining indigent citizens and those who are unemployed; although those who are employable should not be a constitutional responsibility of municipal or provincial governments.
I have gone over the report of the national employment commission, and find in it a table showing municipal indebtedness, that tremendous burden of municipal debt which has so increased taxation that it is now almost impossible for the municipalities to meet their social needs. In 1926 the gross total bonded indebtedness of municipalities in Canada amounted to 81,050,206,121. There had been a substantial increase from year to year, until in 1934 the debt rose to $1,452,850,562.
An analysis of current developments in Canadian municipal finance points to the following facts:
I may say that this was prepared for the dominion conference of mayors at Ottawa in 1936, by H. Carl Goldenberg:
1.	The duties and responsibilities of municipalities have increased without a proportionate increase in the power to raise the revenue necessary to meet their new obligations ;
2.	Having regard to these increasing duties and responsibilities, real property, the principal source of municipal revenue, is no longer an adequate basis of taxation;
3.	Declining revenues accompanying diminished assessments and increased rates have necessitated a greater resort to borrowing, thereby increasing still further the charge against real property and discouraging new construction and home ownership;
4.	Debt charges and the increasing cost of social services and particularly of unemployment relief are absorbing a continually increasing proportion of annual revenues and are tending to paralyze normal municipal services;
5.	Forced economies in current municipal services are resulting in a huge accumulation of deferred maintenance and expansion.
6.	Having regard to the heavy burden of debt charges, further economies in ordinary expenditures can afford no material relief to the taxpayers of the municipalities.
We find that the debts of the provincial governments are increasing. The reports show that the debts of the provinces have increased from $813,400,000 in 1925 to a total of $1,622,100,000 in 1935. The increase in provincial debt between 1925 and 1929 is given as 22 per cent; between 1929 and 1932, 35 per cent; between 1932 and 1935, 21 per cent; and between 1925 and 1935, there was an increase of 99 per cent.
It should be apparent to anyone who has made a careful analysis of the debt structure of Canada that it is becoming impossible for many municipal and provincial governments to carry out their social responsibilities. They may be constitutionally responsible for the maintenance of their indigent citizens and those who are unemployed; but they find themselves financially unable to carry out their constitutional responsibilities, and now the federal government has cut the relief grants.
The Conservative government, when they were elected in 1930, faced a very serious unemployment problem. That problem was due to a large extent to the policies which had been pursued by the previous Liberal administration during their term of office. I admit that the Conservative party attempted to solve the problem, but they found how impossible that was under the present economic system.
The Liberal government promised to end unemployment in a different way. They promised to abolish poverty, to address themselves to the task of abolishing poverty in this dominion, and they were going to do so by the necessary adjustments in our monetary system so that money and credit could be issued to meet the needs of the people. They recognized that usury, once in control, would wreck any nation, and we therefore naturally expected that the Liberal party would at least make a determined effort to solve the problem of unemployment. When the national employment commission was set up two years ago, the people of Canada expected that they would offer some solution of the unemployment problem, but we find on a careful examination of the report that nothing of a constructive nature has been suggested. True, they have attempted to do something for the youth of this country. Training centres have been established for a small percentage of our unemployed youth, but we have heard nothing from the minister and there is nothing contained in the report that would indicate to the members of the house or the people of Canada what the government intend to do for these youth after they have been trained. There are hundreds and hundreds,

government of a province-the government of Alberta, for example-should suggest to the people of that province that by associating together and controlling their own credit and producing wealth, and being prepared to produce it, they could pay dividends to themselves. We know that it would take an increase in the amount of money to pay dividends to the people; but we know that precautions can be taken to prevent the evils of inflation, and we know also that the velocity of circulation would possibly increase and that it would not take as much as many believe it would to pay a dividend of $25 to every citizen in Canada. We know that if the people of this country were prepared to support the issue of dividends by their willingness to render services and produce wealth, such dividends are possible in this country.
We know that thousands of fishermen on both coasts are on relief; that thousands of fruit growers are not putting in new trees because they are unable to sell the fruit from the trees they have; that our lumber industry has slowed down; that our cement plants are closed or running part time; that our mines in the west are not turning out all the coal which could be produced; that we are not utilizing all the power which is developed in Canada to-day or taking steps to utilize our natural resources to the extent that is possible if our system of economics were properly ordered. We know that physically it is possible to provide the citizens of Canada with a high standard of living, but the present financial system prevents this. People are turning from the present monetary system, realizing that they cannot borrow themselves into prosperity or tax themselves into prosperity.
I turn for a moment to the housing problem. I know that the government attempted to put men back to work by encouraging the erection and repair of homes. Fifteen million dollars have been borrowed from the banks, but what does that amount to in comparison with the tremendous need of housing facilities in this country? Fifteen million dollars could be spent in Montreal alone in slum clearance, and the mess would not be cleared up. I expected, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said before the election that money would be appropriated for a national housing scheme, that money would be issued by the Bank of Canada in sufficient amount really to solve this problem. But that did not take place. On the contrary, an agreement was entered into with the private banks whereby $50,000,000 could be loaned to the people of CanfMr. Landeryou.]
ada at a rate of 6-32 per cent interest, although in the great republic to the south and in New Zealand money for this purpose is provided at four per cent and less. Not only did we allow the private banks to collect 6-32 per cent interest, adding to the private debts of this country, but we guaranteed them against loss up to $15,000,000. The government is throwing the responsibility for the unemployed upon the individual citizens of the country, asking them to go further into debt without assuring them that the government is taking steps to remove this paradox of starvation in the midst of plenty.
I hope the news we hear is true, namely that the minister intends to bring down a bill which will provide for more than a mere alleviation of the situation, for something of a permanent nature, a real attack on this problem. If he engages in a scheme of public works, and if other departments of the government encourage industry, develop foreign trade, explore every possible avenue to improve the employment situation, I believe that it will not be necessary to carry on such public works indefinitely; that the time will come when public works can slacken off, because these men will become absorbed in industry. But until such time as industry is able to absorb all the unemployed who are employable, it is the duty and responsibility of the government to provide for their needs -and not with borrowed money. It is time for the government to take over the issue and control of money, not to wait for seven years or for any other period. It is not sufficient to have control of fifty-one per cent of the shares of the Bank of Canada, or to have the power to appoint a majority of the board of directors. What we want is a government which will change the policy of that bank, and take control of the issue of money and credit and so order it that there will be sufficient for those who need it in industry, and sufficient purchasing power in the hands of the people to enable them to buy the products of industry and "the services which can be rendered by the citizens of Canada to each other.
The minister referred to relief rates. He said the employment commission had recommended that some of these rates be cut down.
